questions.question: Which of the following best defines a scalar quantity?
options: A quantity with magnitude, direction, and obeying vector laws.
A quantity with only magnitude and no specific direction.
A quantity with magnitude but obeying parallelogram law.
A quantity with direction but lacking a physical magnitude.
questions.explanation:
A scalar quantity is a physical quantity that is completely specified by its magnitude alone — it has no direction. Examples include mass, time, temperature, speed, distance, and energy.

• Option A describes a vector.
• Option C is inconsistent — the parallelogram law is for vector addition.
• Option D describes a direction without magnitude, which is not a physical scalar.

questions.question: Which of the following best defines a vector quantity?
options: A physical quantity having only magnitude and a unit.
A physical quantity completely described by magnitude.
A physical quantity having magnitude and direction.
A physical quantity having neither magnitude nor direction.
questions.explanation:
A vector quantity is a physical quantity that has both magnitude and direction and obeys the laws of vector algebra (e.g., the parallelogram law of addition). Examples include displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, and momentum.

Options A, B, and D either describe scalars or non-physical constructs.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a scalar quantity?
questions.explanation:
Speed is a scalar because it is the magnitude of velocity — it tells you how fast something is moving, but not in which direction.

• Displacement is a vector (change in position).
• Acceleration is a vector (rate of change of velocity).
• Momentum is a vector (mass × velocity).

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a vector quantity?
questions.explanation:
Displacement is a vector — it is the straight-line distance from the starting point to the ending point, together with the direction of that line.

• Mass, time, and temperature are scalars; they have magnitude only.

questions.question: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.explanation:
Weight is the gravitational force acting on a body (W = mg). It is a force, and force is a vector — it has magnitude and is directed toward the centre of the Earth.

• Speed and distance are scalars.
• Mass is a scalar.

questions.question: A physical quantity that has a magnitude but no direction is a:
questions.explanation: By definition, a scalar has magnitude only. A vector has both magnitude and direction. A tensor is a more general mathematical object. A resultant is the single vector equivalent to the sum of two or more vectors.

questions.question: Distance and displacement are examples of:
questions.explanation: Distance is the total path length travelled — it has magnitude only, so it is a scalar. Displacement is the change in position in a specific direction — it is a vector.

questions.question: A vector is represented by a directed line segment where the length indicates:
questions.explanation: In a vector diagram, a vector is drawn as an arrow. The length of the arrow represents the magnitude of the vector (to scale), while the arrowhead shows its direction.

questions.question: Equal vectors must:
options: Have the same magnitude but different directions.
Have the same direction but different magnitudes.
Have the same magnitude and the same direction.
Have opposite directions and different magnitudes.
questions.explanation: Two vectors are equal if and only if they have the same magnitude and the same direction. Their starting points do not matter (they are free vectors).

questions.question: The negative of a vector has:
options: The exact same direction and magnitude.
The same magnitude but opposite direction.
A different magnitude and same direction.
No magnitude and an undefined direction.
questions.explanation: The negative of a vector A, written −A, has the same magnitude but the opposite direction. This is essential for defining vector subtraction: A − B = A + (−B).

questions.question: What is a null vector?
options: Has a magnitude of exactly zero.
Has a specific direction but no magnitude.
Has a magnitude of exactly one.
Is always equal in length to a unit vector.
questions.explanation: A null vector (or zero vector) has magnitude zero and an arbitrary direction. It is the identity element for vector addition: A + 0 = A.

questions.question: What is a unit vector?
questions.explanation: A unit vector has magnitude exactly one. It is used to specify direction. Examples: î, ĵ, k̂ along the x, y, and z axes.

questions.question: What is the direction of a unit vector?
options: It is always along the x-axis.
It is always along the y-axis.
It is along the original vector.
It is perpendicular to the original vector.
questions.explanation: A unit vector obtained from a vector A points in the same direction as A. It is defined as A-hat = A / |A|, where |A| is the magnitude of A.

questions.question: The magnitude of a unit vector is:
questions.explanation: By definition, a unit vector has magnitude one. This is what distinguishes it from other vectors.

questions.question: A unit vector in the direction of vector A is denoted as:
questions.explanation: The unit vector in the direction of A is written as A-hat (A with a caret). It equals A divided by its magnitude: A-hat = A/|A|.

questions.question: Which type of vector has a direction but no specific spatial origin?
questions.explanation: A free vector is a vector whose initial point is not fixed — it can be translated anywhere in space without changing its magnitude or direction. A position vector is a bound vector (fixed at the origin).

questions.question: Multiplying a vector by -1 will:
questions.explanation: Multiplying a vector by −1 reverses its direction but keeps its magnitude the same: −A has magnitude |A| but points opposite to A.

questions.question: The resultant of two vectors is found using:
options: Always equals the algebraic sum of their magnitudes.
Is found using the parallelogram law.
Is always smaller than the smallest vector.
Has no relation to the original vectors' directions.
questions.explanation: The resultant of two vectors is found graphically using the parallelogram law (or equivalently, the triangle law). It is the diagonal of the parallelogram formed by the two vectors drawn from a common point.

questions.question: Vector addition is commutative, which means:
questions.explanation: Vector addition is commutative: the order in which you add two vectors does not affect the resultant, so A + B = B + A.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about vector addition?
options: It depends on the path taken.
questions.explanation: Vector addition is associative: (A + B) + C = A + (B + C). It is also commutative. It does not depend on the path (it is path-independent). The result is a vector, not a scalar.

questions.question: The triangle law of vector addition requires vectors to be drawn:
options: Vectors are drawn perpendicular to each other.
questions.explanation: The triangle law of vector addition states that if two vectors are represented in magnitude and direction by two sides of a triangle taken in order (i.e., head-to-tail), then their resultant is represented by the third side taken in the reverse order.

questions.question: The sum of a vector and its negative vector is:
questions.explanation: For any vector A, A + (−A) = 0, the null vector. This is the additive inverse property of vectors.

questions.question: The resultant of two vectors is maximum when the angle between them is:
questions.explanation: The magnitude of the resultant is R = √(A² + B² + 2AB cos θ). This is maximum when cos θ = 1, i.e., θ = 0° (the vectors point in the same direction). Then R = A + B.

questions.question: The resultant of two vectors is minimum when the angle between them is:
questions.explanation: R = √(A² + B² + 2AB cos θ). This is minimum when cos θ = −1, i.e., θ = 180° (vectors point in opposite directions). Then R = |A − B|.

questions.question: The dot product of two vectors results in a:
options: Is always equal to exactly zero.
questions.explanation: The dot product (scalar product) of two vectors A·B = |A||B|cos θ produces a scalar. It is used to find the angle between vectors and to compute work (W = F·d).

questions.question: The cross product of two vectors results in a:
options: Is always equal to exactly zero.
Is always parallel to both vectors.
questions.explanation: The cross product (vector product) A×B = |A||B|sin θ n̂ produces a vector that is perpendicular to both A and B (direction given by the right-hand rule).

questions.question: The dot product of two perpendicular vectors is:
questions.explanation: If two vectors are perpendicular, θ = 90°, and cos 90° = 0, so A·B = |A||B|cos 90° = 0. This is a key test for perpendicularity.

questions.question: The cross product of two parallel vectors is:
questions.explanation: If two vectors are parallel (or anti-parallel), θ = 0° or 180°, and sin θ = 0, so A×B = 0 (the null vector).

questions.question: The direction of the cross product of two vectors is:
options: Along the bisector of the two vectors.
In the same plane as the two vectors.
questions.explanation: The cross product A×B is always perpendicular to both A and B — that is, it is perpendicular to the plane containing A and B.

questions.question: The direction of the cross product of two vectors is given by the:
questions.explanation: The direction of A×B is determined by the right-hand rule: point the fingers of your right hand along A, curl them toward B, and your thumb points in the direction of A×B.

questions.question: The magnitude of the cross product is given by:
questions.explanation: The magnitude of the cross product is |A×B| = |A||B|sin θ, where θ is the angle between the two vectors.

questions.question: The magnitude of the dot product is given by:
questions.explanation: The dot product is A·B = |A||B|cos θ, where θ is the angle between the vectors. Its magnitude is |A||B|cos θ.

questions.question: The dot product of two vectors is also known as the:
questions.explanation: The dot product is also called the scalar product because its result is a scalar. The cross product is called the vector product.

questions.question: If A · B = 0, the angle between A and B is:
questions.explanation: A·B = |A||B|cos θ = 0. Since |A| and |B| are not zero (for non-null vectors), cos θ = 0, so θ = 90°. The vectors are perpendicular.

questions.question: If A × B = 0, the vectors are:
questions.explanation: A×B = |A||B|sin θ n̂ = 0. This requires sin θ = 0, so θ = 0° or 180°, meaning the vectors are parallel (or anti-parallel).
